The word "flip-flop" has three distinct meanings — one everyday, one social/political, and one technical. Each meaning is unrelated to the others in terms of usage, but they all share a common underlying idea, which I'll point out at the end.

The most common, everyday meaning of "flip-flop" is a simple, flat, open sandal.

It has a flat sole — the part your foot rests on — and a single strap shaped like the letter Y or V. This strap passes between your big toe and the toe next to it, anchoring the sandal to your foot. That's it. There's no back support, no laces, no buckle.

Flip-flops are extremely casual footwear. You can slip them on and off in seconds. They're popular at beaches, swimming pools, and in warm or tropical climates. Because they leave your feet largely uncovered, they are generally not considered appropriate for formal occasions, offices, or smart-casual settings in many cultures.

The name "flip-flop" is onomatopoeic — it imitates the sound the sandal makes. As you walk, the sole slaps rhythmically against your heel: flip... flop... flip... flop. That slapping sound gave the sandal its name.

You might also know these sandals by other regional names: thongs in Australia, slippers in parts of South and Southeast Asia, jandals in New Zealand, or chappal in South Asia.
Meaning 2: A sudden reversal of opinion or position

In everyday English — especially in politics, journalism, and public debate — a "flip-flop" means a sudden, complete reversal of a previously stated position, belief, or decision.

Think of a coin lying flat. It has two sides: heads and tails. Now imagine it being flipped over. That image captures the idea perfectly: a person goes from holding one position entirely to holding the opposite position.

Example: A politician campaigns on the promise "I will never raise taxes." Two years later, she supports and votes for a tax increase. People would say she "did a flip-flop" — or that her stance was a flip-flop.

The word carries a strongly negative tone. Calling something a flip-flop implies that the person is inconsistent, untrustworthy, or opportunistic — that they changed their position not out of honest reflection, but out of political pressure, personal gain, or a desire to please a different audience. It's an accusation of unreliability.

This is an important distinction: a flip-flop is not the same as a genuine change of mind. If someone says, "I used to oppose this policy, but after learning new evidence, I now support it," that is seen as intellectual honesty — it wouldn't typically be called a flip-flop. The term "flip-flop" is reserved for reversals that appear sudden, self-serving, or unexplained.

The word is most frequently used in political commentary and journalism, but it appears in everyday conversation too. For instance: "Last week you said you wanted to take a road trip. Now you want to fly. You keep flip-flopping on the plan!"

This is the most technical of the three meanings. It belongs to the world of electronics and computer science.

In digital electronics, a flip-flop is a type of circuit — and one of the most fundamentally important ones in all of computing.

First, a bit of background

Digital electronics deals entirely in two values: 0 and 1. You can think of these as "off" and "on," or "low voltage" and "high voltage." Every operation inside a computer — calculations, storing data, displaying images — ultimately comes down to processing enormous quantities of 0s and 1s.

What a flip-flop does

A flip-flop is a circuit that can exist in exactly one of two stable states at any given moment: state 0 or state 1. Once it settles into a state, it stays there — holding that value — until an external electrical signal tells it to switch. When it switches, it goes from 0 to 1 or from 1 to 0. Then it holds that new state, again indefinitely, until told to switch again.

This behavior of alternating between two stable positions is exactly why it's called a "flip-flop."

Why flip-flops matter: memory

Here is the crucial insight: because a flip-flop can hold a value of 0 or 1 — and keep holding it even after the input signal is gone — it acts as a one-bit memory cell.

It sounds simple, but this is profoundly important. A single flip-flop is the most elementary form of digital memory: it remembers one thing (a 0 or a 1). When you group multiple flip-flops together, they form what are called registers — tiny but extremely fast memory units inside a processor (CPU). Registers hold the values that the processor is actively computing with at any instant.

So every time your computer, phone, or any digital device "remembers" a value — even for a microsecond — flip-flops are involved. They are the atoms of digital memory.

Types of flip-flops

Several standard types of flip-flop circuits exist, each with slightly different rules about how and when they change state:

SR flip-flop (Set-Reset): The most basic type. It has two inputs: S (Set) and R (Reset). A signal at S forces the output to 1; a signal at R forces it to 0. One problem: if you signal S and R at the same time, the output becomes undefined and unpredictable — this is called the "forbidden state."

D flip-flop (Data or Delay): Has one data input (D) and a clock input. Each time a clock pulse arrives, the flip-flop "captures" whatever value (0 or 1) is currently present at D and holds it. This eliminates the forbidden-state problem of the SR type, making it far more practical and widely used — especially in registers.

JK flip-flop: A refined version of the SR flip-flop. It cleverly resolves the forbidden-state problem: when both inputs (J and K) are signaled at the same time, instead of behaving unpredictably, the output simply toggles — it flips to whatever state it was not in. This makes it more versatile than the SR type.

T flip-flop (Toggle): Has a single input, T. When T is 1 and a clock pulse arrives, the output flips to the opposite state (0 becomes 1, or 1 becomes 0). When T is 0, the output stays unchanged. This is the simplest toggling behavior possible, and it is especially useful in building counters — circuits that count clock pulses.

Despite their differences, all four types share the same core property: two stable states, the ability to switch between them on command, and the ability to hold the current state in between commands.

Less commonly, "flip-flop" is used informally in gymnastics and acrobatics to describe a back handspring — a move where a gymnast springs backward, plants their hands on the floor, and flips their legs over to land on their feet again. The move resembles the back-and-forth flipping motion the name suggests. This use is informal and specific to the sport, but worth knowing.
The thread connecting all three meanings

All three primary meanings of "flip-flop" share a single underlying image: switching back and forth between two opposite states.

  • The sandal makes a back-and-forth slapping motion as you walk.
  • The opinion reversal involves switching from one stance to its complete opposite.
  • The electronic circuit switches between the two binary states — 0 and 1.

This idea of a two-state toggle, of going from one extreme to the other, is the conceptual heartbeat of the word in every context it's used.
